record.original_question: Can two lions catch a man in finite time in a bounded planar region containing rectifiable lakes, when all players have equal maximum speeds and capture requires the lion and the man to coincide?

evidence.quote: The princess and monster game is relat ed to the game between the lion and a Christian, which was invented by Richard Rado: a lion and a Christian in a closed circular arena have equal maximum speeds.Can the lion catch the Christian in ﬁnite time? Surprisingly, the answer turns out to be NO [3, p 46], provided that the players are both represented by points, and the radius of detection is zero.

Littlewood in his Miscellany [ 14], and he added the following problem: can two lions catch a man in a bounded area with rectiﬁable lakes? According to Béla Bollobás [ 3], this problem remains unsolved.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a bounded region R in the Euclidean plane whose complement (within some bounding box) consists of finitely many "lakes," each lake being an open set whose boundary is a rectifiable Jordan curve. Three players — two "lions" L_1, L_2 and one "man" M — are modeled as points moving inside the closure of R. All three move along continuous trajectories and have the same maximum speed (normalized to 1); that is, each trajectory is 1-Lipschitz with respect to time. The lions choose their strategy knowing the position of the man at every time, and the man likewise knows the positions of the lions. The lions "capture" the man if at some finite time t ≥ 0 the position of at least one lion coincides with the position of the man.

Question: Do the two lions always have a strategy that guarantees capture of the man in finite time, regardless of the shape of R (subject to the rectifiable-lakes condition) and regardless of the man's strategy?
artifact.status_search_result: The question (originally posed by Littlewood) has been resolved in the negative: there exists a bounded planar region with finitely many rectifiable lakes in which the man has a strategy to evade two lions forever. The same line of work shows that three lions always suffice to capture the man under these conditions, so two lions are not enough in general.

status_evidence.title: Best Laid Plans of Lions and Men
status_evidence.snippet: We show that three lions have a winning strategy against a man in a bounded region with finitely many rectifiable lakes... there exists a region R in the plane where the man has a strategy to survive forever.
status_evidence.claim: Two lions are insufficient (counterexample region exists), while three lions always suffice; this resolves Littlewood's two-lion question negatively.
